You are a Senior Code Reviewer with expertise in software architecture, deployment infrastructure, and best practices. Your job is to review a completed feature branch against its plan and identify issues before merge. This is the FINAL phase of a multi-month project — after this merges, the project's v1 is fully done per its own design doc's stated bar.

## What Was Implemented

`feat/phase10-deployability` — Phase 10 ("deployability") for atlas-fieldforce, a field-force tracking product (FastAPI backend + React manager dashboard + Capacitor Android tablet app, all already built, tested, and merged in prior phases). Three tasks, all individually reviewed already and approved with zero fix rounds across the entire phase:

1. `backend/Dockerfile` + `backend/docker-entrypoint.sh` + `backend/.dockerignore` — multi-stage build (uv/Python builder → slim runtime), entrypoint runs `alembic upgrade head && exec uvicorn ...`. Verified against a real `postgres:16` container (not just SQLite, which is all this project's migrations had ever run against before).
2. `dashboard/Dockerfile` + `dashboard/nginx.conf` + `dashboard/.dockerignore` — multi-stage build (node builder → nginx runtime), custom nginx config for SPA client-side routing (`try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html`).
3. Root `docker-compose.yml` (db + backend + dashboard, `condition: service_healthy` gating) + README additions (Docker quickstart, and an explicit punch list of what still needs a real human/infra decision before going live).

## Requirements / Plan

Full plan: /Users/taha/Documents/atlas-fieldforce/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-21-phase10-deployability.md (read this in full — it has a detailed Global Constraints section with the binding design decisions, the exact per-task file contents, and a pre-plan spike section documenting what was verified empirically before any code was written).

`docs/design.md` (read the "Deployable vs deployed" section near the end, and the "Location pings at scale" / "Offline" / "Background location on Android" / "Alerts" / "Deferred to the merge-into-Atlas phase" / "Non-functional" sections) is the actual source-of-truth spec this whole project has been built against — Phase 10's job is closing the LAST bar it sets: *"v1 done means: Dockerfile/compose, CI green, migrations run clean, tests pass, backend+dashboard buildable, tablet APK buildable. It does not mean provisioning paid cloud infra, deploying to a live customer-facing environment, or sending real push notifications — those need explicit sign-off."*

## Git Range to Review

**Base (merge-base with main):** 6d2fb7db4527c79d8837588bb8a2b9eb6d232758
**Head:** current HEAD of branch feat/phase10-deployability

A pre-generated diff package is at /Users/taha/Documents/atlas-fieldforce/.superpowers/sdd/review-6d2fb7d..6880e7f.diff — read it once. You may also read any file in the repo directly for broader context.

## Read-Only Review... EXCEPT for one thing

Your review is read-only on this checkout (/Users/taha/Documents/atlas-fieldforce, branch feat/phase10-deployability) — do not mutate the git working tree, index, HEAD, or branch state in any way.

**However, this phase's entire subject matter is Docker infrastructure, and every one of its 3 task-level reviews already independently ran real `docker build`/`docker compose up` verification rather than trusting reports — you should too, if you want confidence beyond re-reading what three prior reviewers already confirmed.** Docker is available in this environment (`colima`; run `colima start` first if `docker ps` fails — colima has been running throughout this phase's work already). You're welcome to run `docker compose up -d --build` from the repo root yourself and hit the same three checks every prior reviewer ran (register through the backend, dashboard `/`, dashboard `/zones`) if you want first-hand confidence rather than relying on three separate task reviewers' already-thorough independent verification — but this is optional here specifically because that verification has already happened three times over at the task level (Task 1's reviewer used `docker top` to confirm PID 1; Task 2's reviewer rebuilt with `--no-cache` and a deliberately different build-arg value to rule out cache-hit coincidences; Task 3's reviewer ran a full fresh `docker compose up` and grepped the compiled bundle). Your marginal value-add is more likely in catching something ACROSS the 3 tasks that no single task-scoped review could see, or in the non-Docker parts (README accuracy, PLAN.md/PROGRESS.md correctness, whether this really closes out the full v1 scope) — weight your effort accordingly, but don't skip a real verification run if anything in the diff gives you a specific reason to doubt a claim.

## What to Check

**Plan alignment:** Does the implementation match the plan's Global Constraints and per-task specs? Any unjustified deviations?

**Cross-task integration** (this is the review layer that only exists at this level, not in any single task's review): Do the three pieces actually cohere as ONE deployable system, not just three independently-correct pieces? E.g., does the `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` the backend service is configured with in `docker-compose.yml` actually match the origin the dashboard is served from? Would a `docker compose up` from a genuinely fresh clone (no locally-cached images, no prior manual Docker state) actually work, or does anything in this phase quietly depend on state left over from the individual task verifications?

**Code quality:** Dockerfile/compose/nginx conventions, no obvious security footguns for what's meant to be a LOCAL dev/deployability proof (not a production hardening pass — design.md's own bar explicitly excludes production hardening from this phase's scope, so don't hold this to a production-security bar it was never meant to meet, but do flag anything that would be actively wrong even for that lower bar).

**Testing:** Was verification real (actual containers, actual requests) at every layer, or did anything get asserted without being run?

**Documentation accuracy:** Is the new README content and the PROGRESS.md entry accurate to what was actually built and verified, not aspirational or overstated? Does the punch list actually cover what's left, or is anything missing that a real deployer would hit?

**Production readiness relative to design.md's own stated bar** (not a higher bar than that): does this genuinely close PLAN.md 10.1/10.2/10.3, and does the whole project now genuinely meet design.md's "deployable vs deployed" definition?

## Calibration

Categorize issues by actual severity. Acknowledge what's done well before listing issues. If you find issues with the PLAN itself (not just the implementation), say so explicitly.

## Output Format

### Strengths

### Issues

#### Critical (Must Fix)
#### Important (Should Fix)
#### Minor (Nice to Have)

For each issue: file:line, what's wrong, why it matters, how to fix.

### Recommendations

### Assessment

**Ready to merge?** [Yes | No | With fixes]
**Reasoning:** [1-2 sentence technical assessment]

**Does this genuinely complete v1 per design.md's own bar?** [Yes | No | With caveats — name them]

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

2	
3	> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

5	**Goal:** The last phase before v1 is "done" per `docs/design.md`'s own exact bar (line 75): *"Dockerfile/compose, CI green, migrations run clean, tests pass, backend+dashboard buildable, tablet APK buildable. It does **not** mean provisioning paid cloud infra, deploying to a live customer-facing environment, or sending real push notifications — those need explicit sign-off."* CI green, tests passing, and both apps buildable are already true (Phases 1-9). This phase adds the one missing piece — Dockerfile(s) + compose, with migrations verified against REAL Postgres (every migration in this project has, until now, only ever run against SQLite in tests) — plus a README quickstart and an explicit punch list of what still needs a human decision (domain, VAPID keys, cloud provider, real-device GPS testing, and everything else design.md itself already named as deferred).
6	
7	**Environment facts, verified empirically before this plan was written:**
8	- **Docker is available via `colima`, but colima was not running at session start** (`docker ps` failed with "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon"). Every session that touches Docker in this environment needs `colima start` first if `docker ps` fails — this is a one-time-per-cold-environment step, not something to script into the app itself.
9	- **All 9 existing migrations were run against a real, throwaway `postgres:16` container for the first time in this project's history and applied cleanly with zero errors** — including the trickiest one (`cb47af5f6a3a`, the visits idempotency-key migration, which needed `op.batch_alter_table` specifically because SQLite can't `ALTER` a constraint directly; Alembic's batch mode is forward-compatible and just runs a direct `ALTER TABLE` on Postgres, confirmed by inspecting the resulting real table via `psql \d visits` — the unique constraint, both FKs, and all indexes are present and correctly named). This was a real, previously-unverified risk (every prior "verified via SQLite PRAGMA" claim in this project's history was SQLite-only) — now closed.
10	- **A live app boot + real HTTP request against that same Postgres container also succeeded** (`POST /api/v1/auth/register` → 201, real JWT tokens returned) — proving the `asyncpg` driver path works end-to-end at the ORM/query level, not just that migrations apply.
11	- **Vite bakes `VITE_API_BASE_URL` into the built JS bundle at BUILD time**, not runtime (`import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL` is a static replacement, same as the dashboard's existing pattern) — the dashboard's Dockerfile MUST pass this as a Docker build `ARG` (set before the `npm run build` step), not a container runtime `ENV`. Setting it as a runtime-only env var on the built container would silently have no effect (the value baked into the JS at build time wins) — this is the one genuine Docker+Vite gotcha in this task, named here so it isn't rediscovered the hard way.
12	- **`backend/uv.lock` exists** (confirmed via `ls`) — the backend Dockerfile can use `uv sync --frozen` for reproducible installs.
13	- **`ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.11.21` is a real, currently-published image tag** (verified via `docker manifest inspect`, matching this environment's installed `uv --version` — 0.11.21 — so the containerized build uses the same `uv` version already proven to work in this repo, not an unrelated pin).
14	- **The app has no auto-migration-on-boot logic** (`backend/app/main.py`'s `lifespan` only starts the in-process retention job runner) — migrations must be run as an explicit step before `uvicorn` starts. `backend/alembic/env.py` already reads `DATABASE_URL` from `app.config.get_settings()` — the same env var the app itself uses — so a container entrypoint just needs `DATABASE_URL` set correctly and can run `alembic upgrade head` directly with no extra wiring.
15	- **`backend/docker-compose.yml` already exists** (Postgres-only, for non-Docker local dev — `uv run uvicorn` against a containerized DB) and stays exactly as-is; this phase does NOT modify it. A NEW root-level `docker-compose.yml` is added for the full containerized stack (db + backend + dashboard) — the two serve different, both-still-valid workflows (quick local dev vs. "does the whole thing actually run in Docker").
16	
17	## Global Constraints
18	
19	- **Multi-stage Docker builds for both `backend/Dockerfile` and `dashboard/Dockerfile`** — a build stage with the full toolchain (uv/Python, or Node/npm), a slim runtime stage that only copies the built artifact. This is the standard, correct pattern (smaller final image, no build toolchain in the image that actually runs), not gold-plating.
20	- **Backend image runs migrations via an entrypoint script (`backend/docker-entrypoint.sh`), then execs uvicorn** — `alembic upgrade head && exec uvicorn app.main:create_app --factory --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000`. Using `exec` (not a plain shell call) so uvicorn becomes PID 1 and receives signals correctly for clean container shutdown — a real correctness detail, not stylistic.
21	- **Dashboard image is nginx serving the Vite build output, with a custom nginx config for SPA client-side routing** (`try_files $uri /index.html;`) — without this, a manager who directly navigates to (or refreshes on) `/zones`, `/tasks`, etc. gets a raw nginx 404, since those paths only exist client-side via `react-router`'s `BrowserRouter`. This is a real, easily-missed gap for any SPA served via a generic static file server, not a hypothetical.
22	- **The root `docker-compose.yml`'s `backend` service depends on `db` via `condition: service_healthy`** (a `pg_isready` healthcheck on the `db` service), not a bare `depends_on: [db]` — a bare dependency only waits for the container to START, not for Postgres to actually be ready to accept connections, which would make `alembic upgrade head` in the entrypoint racy. **Environment facts, verified empirically before this plan was written:**
- **Docker is available via `colima`, but colima was not running at session start** (`docker ps` failed with "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon"). Every session that touches Docker in this environment needs `colima start` first if `docker ps` fails — this is a one-time-per-cold-environment step, not something to script into the app itself.
- **All 9 existing migrations were run against a real, throwaway `postgres:16` container for the first time in this project's history and applied cleanly with zero errors** — including the trickiest one (`cb47af5f6a3a`, the visits idempotency-key migration, which needed `op.batch_alter_table` specifically because SQLite can't `ALTER` a constraint directly; Alembic's batch mode is forward-compatible and just runs a direct `ALTER TABLE` on Postgres, confirmed by inspecting the resulting real table via `psql \d visits` — the unique constraint, both FKs, and all indexes are present and correctly named). This was a real, previously-unverified risk (every prior "verified via SQLite PRAGMA" claim in this project's history was SQLite-only) — now closed.
- **A live app boot + real HTTP request against that same Postgres container also succeeded** (`POST /api/v1/auth/register` → 201, real JWT tokens returned) — proving the `asyncpg` driver path works end-to-end at the ORM/query level, not just that migrations apply.
- **Vite bakes `VITE_API_BASE_URL` into the built JS bundle at BUILD time**, not runtime (`import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL` is a static replacement, same as the dashboard's existing pattern) — the dashboard's Dockerfile MUST pass this as a Docker build `ARG` (set before the `npm run build` step), not a container runtime `ENV`. Setting it as a runtime-only env var on the built container would silently have no effect (the value baked into the JS at build time wins) — this is the one genuine Docker+Vite gotcha in this task, named here so it isn't rediscovered the hard way.
- **`backend/uv.lock` exists** (confirmed via `ls`) — the backend Dockerfile can use `uv sync --frozen` for reproducible installs.

- **Multi-stage Docker builds for both `backend/Dockerfile` and `dashboard/Dockerfile`** — a build stage with the full toolchain (uv/Python, or Node/npm), a slim runtime stage that only copies the built artifact. This is the standard, correct pattern (smaller final image, no build toolchain in the image that actually runs), not gold-plating.

## Geofencing

Zones are GeoJSON polygons; point-in-polygon is a small pure-Python check in the service layer — **not PostGIS**. Checks are always against one rep's small assigned-zone set, not a tenant-wide spatial search, so DB-level spatial indexing isn't needed, and this keeps tests SQLite-compatible instead of adding a heavy DB extension as a day-one dependency.

## Location pings at scale (500+ reps/tenant)

Single `location_pings` table sized for volume from the start; a background retention job (in-process job runner, same pattern as Atlas's `core/jobs`) prunes raw pings after ~30 days and downsamples older data. No new infra beyond a scheduled in-process job.

## Real-time model

Periodic refresh, not push: tablet posts a location ping every 15–60s; manager dashboard polls on an interval. No WebSocket/SSE infrastructure.

## Offline

Tablet queues pings, check-ins, task updates, and photos locally (Capacitor storage plugin) with a client-generated idempotency key per queued item, synced on reconnect — same idempotency-key pattern Atlas requires on document-creating endpoints, so a replayed sync can't double-count a visit.

## Background location on Android — decision needed before building the tablet client

The robust, most-used Capacitor background-geolocation plugin (Transistorsoft) is **commercially licensed**, not free. Default to the open-source path — `@capacitor-community/background-geolocation` plus an Android foreground service — and accept its rougher edges (battery optimization fights, less polish) rather than take on a per-deployment license cost without the customer signing off on it. Flag this explicitly if background tracking proves unreliable enough that the paid plugin becomes the right call.

## Alerts

`ZoneViolationDetected` domain event → handler sends a web push (VAPID, `pywebpush`) to subscribed managers' browsers, and the violation shows on the dashboard regardless. Note: browser web push is not self-contained — it routes through Google's FCM, needs HTTPS and a registered service worker, and can't be fully exercised end-to-end without real deployment infrastructure (this is a "needs real infra to verify" item, not something local dev proves out).

## Deferred to the merge-into-Atlas phase

Real CRM/Sales linking (live FK instead of free-text reference), reading real Sales order values for `SALES_VALUE` goals, folding `reps` into Atlas's HR `employees`, Atlas's full RBAC/permission-catalog, multi-tenant UX.

## Non-functional

Tests mirror source structure. List endpoints ≤3 queries, paginated, indexed hot paths — same bar as Atlas's PERFORMANCE.md. `tests/perf/` budget for the ping-ingestion path given the 500+-rep target.

## "Deployable" vs "deployed"

v1 done means: Dockerfile/compose, CI green, migrations run clean, tests pass, backend+dashboard buildable, tablet APK buildable. It does **not** mean provisioning paid cloud infra, deploying to a live customer-facing environment, or sending real push notifications — those need explicit sign-off (cost, domain, credentials) before happening.
